Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is the most decisive document in the set, and mostly a well-calibrated one. It tests the disputed claims directly: it pre-registers the mediation test, adds a stricter hours measure, and reports the counter-arm failure and the Halden reversions plainly. Its treatment of the two earlier overclaims in §5 is fair to both.

My concerns are mostly about how specific numbers are presented and interpreted. Two of them affect the paper's own conclusions: the decline in the per-hour gain is partly a change on the control side, and "confirms" overstates the mediation result.

## Arithmetic check

Everything I checked reconciles:
- **Varden, logs:** 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5%.
- **Varden, timesheets:** 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8%.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100%.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 / 40.3 is a fall of 13.4%, and 96.8 / 86.6 = +11.8%.

## Main points

**1. The summary compares different measures as if they showed a change over time.**
The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." But 12.5% is a timesheet figure and 8.5% is a system-log figure. On the same measure, the decline is from 12.5% to 9.8%, about 22%. The body gets this right ("on the like-for-like timesheet measure"), but the summary blends a change of measure with a change over time. §5's "declined by about a quarter" is also a little generous; "about a fifth" is closer.

**2. Part of the "decay" happened in the control group.**
In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their own meetings and raised output per hour by 4.1%. That lifts the control mean by roughly 1.2 points, which is a meaningful share of the 2.7-point fall in the difference. Some of the apparent fading is therefore the comparison group catching up, not the treated offices slipping.

The report presents this episode as evidence about reorganising without cutting hours. It doesn't connect it to the decay estimate. The authors should split the difference-in-differences change into its treated and control trends, and show the 24-month estimate with and without the two offices that held meeting audits.

This matters for what the 24-month figure means:
- *Including* those offices, it estimates the effect of an hours cut against a control group that partly reorganised anyway, which is realistic.
- *Excluding* them, it estimates the effect against a control group that didn't reorganise.

Both are worth reporting.

**3. "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation result.**
The body's wording, "survives a registered test," is right. The summary's "confirms" is not.
- **Untestable assumptions.** Mediation depends on there being no unmeasured confounding between the mediators and the outcome. The obvious confounder is manager quality: managers who cut meetings may also improve the work in other ways. The limitations section mentions the assumption but doesn't name this risk.
- **Effective sample size.** There are 14 clusters. "Office-months" add repeated measurements, not independent offices. An interval of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters and an imprecise total effect (3.4 to 13.8). Proportions mediated are unstable when the denominator is uncertain, and the method for the interval should be stated.
- **Overlap with the data that generated the hypothesis.** The test was registered at month 11 but appears to use mediator data from baseline onward. That includes the months behind the exploratory finding. A cleaner confirmatory test would use months 12–24 only.
- **The mediators interact.** Fewer meetings may reduce fatigue, so how the gain is shared between the two pathways depends on the model. Say how the joint model handles this.

**4. Two data-provenance questions need answers.**
- **Baseline meeting time.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected *in month six*, as levels only. This report gives baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours). If these were recovered from historical calendars, say so. This matters because it is exactly what turns the earlier comparison of levels into an actual reduction.
- **Baseline log data.** The log-based hours measure was "added" at follow-up. A difference-in-differences needs pre-period log hours. Were historical logs available for both arms?

**5. "Stricter" hours measure? Log time is different, not strictly better.**
Active log-in time captures unclaimed work done on the system. It misses work done off the system: phone calls, paper files, and meetings themselves. It isn't a superset of timesheet hours.

This creates an interpretive puzzle for the mediation. If meeting time isn't in the log-hour denominator, cutting meetings can't raise output per log-hour simply by removing unproductive hours. It must work through something else, such as fewer interruptions and longer stretches of focused work. That is a plausible and interesting mechanism, but it differs from the "removing low-value time" story, and the report should say which one it supports.

**6. Service quality in case-processing is still incomplete.**
The nine-month limitations raised the question of whether backlogs build up beyond statutory deadlines. The 24-month report gives appeal overturn rates but not time to decision, backlog size, or deadline compliance. It's the most obvious remaining question for the stratum that "worked."

**7. The Halden follow-up needs two corrections.**
- **One reversion doesn't fit the coverage explanation.** The summary says all reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations." But a marketing agency citing *client deadlines* would be classed as discretionary work under the meta-analysis's scheme. So one of three reversions happened in the kind of work where reduced hours is supposed to suit. That is a modest counterexample to the clean split by work type, and should be noted rather than folded in.
- **Response selection adds a third filter.** Only 14 of 23 organisations agreed to take part. The 11 continuers are survivors three times over: they completed the pilot, chose to continue, and agreed to respond. Calling the estimate an upper bound is right, and should be stated with this extra filter.

**8. The original Halden attrition problem goes unaddressed.**
R. Okafor, a Halden author, co-authors this report. The re-analysis found that seven of the nine Halden withdrawals happened *after* the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons. The working paper had said they withdrew during preparation for scheduling reasons. This follow-up is the natural place to acknowledge and correct that, and it says nothing.

## Smaller points
- **Sick days.** The −27% figure still doesn't say whether it is per scheduled day. It may be inflated by exposure, the same issue raised in each earlier round.
- **Resignations.** These are still compared as levels, without confidence intervals.
- **Counter-arm costs.** A 12% increase in staff yielding only a 9% rise in cost per contact implies contacts would rise by about 3%. That's plausible, given fewer abandoned calls, but the assumption should be stated.

## Where the evidence now stands

| Question | Before this report | After |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | About 8–10%, durability unknown | **About 8.5–10% at 24 months in the one randomised study**; part of the decline reflects control offices reorganising |
| Per-worker output | Slight decline in controlled studies | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2): the hours cut is mostly, not fully, offset |
| Coverage-bound work | Output falls | Arm ended. Restoring service would need about 12% more staff and about 9% higher cost per contact |
| Novelty | Disputed | Some fading, not collapse. "Entirely novelty" and "no decay" are both contradicted |
| Mechanism | Untested | Meetings supported as the largest measured pathway, under untestable assumptions; fatigue smaller; a third unexplained |
| Can reorganisation alone capture the gain? | Not asked | Open. Suggestive evidence from two control offices, with no arm designed to test it |

That last row is now the most policy-relevant open question. If cutting meetings delivers much of the gain, employers could pursue it without cutting hours. Or the hours cut may be what makes such changes happen and last. A trial with a third arm, reorganisation without an hours cut, would settle it.

Across the sequence, this document is the first to correct both earlier overshoots without overshooting itself, except in the wording of its summary. The fixes are mostly editorial: compare like-for-like in the summary, replace "confirms" with "supports," and split the decay into its treated and control components.

I can draft those revisions, or a consolidated evidence brief covering all five reports.
